channel.title: The Dig — Software stack: compilers and pulse level
channel.description: Papers relevant to operating, benchmarking, integrating and using a semiconductor spin-qubit quantum computer of at least 16 qubits that is co-located with and integrated into an HPC system. Today's arXiv announcement, ranked against the Software stack: compilers and pulse level preset. Today’s ranked reading list centers on silicon spin-qubit hardware and operational benchmarking: 2611.12850 proposes over-gate TiN stressors to enhance valley splitting in Si/SiGe wiggle-well dots, 2611.14114 offers a cloud-executed GHZ-fidelity benchmark that tests whether calibration data predict processor performance, and 2611.12217 maps how multi-dot configurations affect electron temperature and double-dot latching for initialization and readout. The skim-tier items broaden the context but sit further from current spin-qubit operation: 2611.13301 presents an MLIR-based fault-tolerant compiler, 2611.12779 a neutral-atom arbitrary two-qubit gate architecture, 2611.13371 silicon-spin qLDPC syndrome extraction with mobile ancillas, 2611.14422 a QRAM energetic-cost accounting method, and 2611.13796 an analog Rydberg-atom QAOA MaxCut study. No pay dirt today — 3 to skim.

item.title: A Compiler for Fault Tolerant Quantum Computing
item.description:
Skim new method — FTQC provides an MLIR dialect with an ECC-aware type system; on the 20-qubit Pathfinder device, decoding lowered logical readout error by a factor of 3.3.

Grade 0.553 · 2.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Noise-Adaptive Compiler Mappings for Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum Computers” · Narasinga Rao Miniskar, Elaine Wong, Seyong Lee, Vicente Leyton-Ortega, Jeffrey S. Vetter, Travis S. Humble

Figure

In-pipeline compile time (parse plus passes) as a function of logical qubit count n across six benchmark circuit families. Near-linear families execute in under 6 ms at n=100, while QFT scales quadratically to 100 ms at n=51.

Asks

How can a quantum compiler preserve error-correcting code information and resource constraints while lowering logical circuits to physical backends?

But

Logical error estimates use leading-order model; distillation tracks peak qubits rather than space-time volume; non-Clifford gates replaced with Clifford stand-ins in Stim; no threshold scaling shown.

Tools

MLIR and ODS · OpenQASM 3.0 · QIR · Stim and PyMatching · 20-qubit Pathfinder (ORNL)

Abstract

Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) needs compiler intermediate representations (IRs) that preserve error-correcting-code choices, syndrome information, and non-Clifford resource requirements through analysis, simulation, and hardware lowering. We report practical experience building FTQC, an open-source Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) dialect that makes logical qubits, syndromes, magic states, and Pauli frames typed static single assignment (SSA) values. Its error-correction-aware type system, two-level lowering design, and IR-resident resource analysis provide one inspectable pipeline to Open Quantum Assembly Language~3 (OpenQASM~3), the Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR), Stim, and IQM hardware. Case studies across three code families show that typed metadata makes code-specific decisions verifiable and retargetable: on the 20-qubit Pathfinder at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, decoding reduced logical readout error by 3.3 times. They also expose hidden architectural costs: for a three-qubit Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT-3), a magic-state factory requires five times the peak qubits of the encoded circuit. These experiences demonstrate a practical foundation for developing and evaluating fault-tolerant compiler transformations across software and hardware targets.

item.title: Unified architecture for arbitrary two-qubit gates with neutral atoms
item.description:
Skim new method — Unified Rydberg-atom architecture realizes arbitrary two-qubit gates natively from an XXZ interaction by tuning the anisotropy Jz/J∈[−1,0] via an RF-dressed Förster resonance and shaping global microwave pulses.

Grade 0.545 · 2.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Qiskit pulse: programming quantum computers through the cloud with pulses”

Figure

Förster defect δF versus dressing frequency fD, and interaction ratio Jz/J alongside Zeeman shift h0 versus δF and atomic separation R, mapping out the required Jz/J∈[−1,0] range.

Asks

Can neutral-atom quantum processors implement the full set of two-qubit gates natively rather than decomposing unitaries into multiple CZ gates?

Before

Generic two-qubit unitaries required three CZ gates interleaved with single-qubit rotations in neutral-atom platforms.

But

Numerical simulation assuming dispersive Rydberg dressing; dressing-state admixture in the computational manifold assumed <10−3; optimization threshold 10−12.

Tools

Ashhab–Nori (AshN) control scheme · RF-dressed Förster resonance · GRAPE quantum optimal control · Rydberg state pair potentials

Abstract

We propose a unified architecture for two-qubit gates in neutral-atom quantum processors which allows the implementation of the complete set of two-qubit gates. Our approach rests on a single resource that unlocks the entire gate set: an XXZ interaction with tunable anisotropy, combined only with single-qubit operations. We introduce a Rydberg-atom realization of the tunable XXZ interaction and combine it with optimally controlled global microwave pulses to implement the B, QFT, iSWAP, and √iSWAP gates, as well as a continuous gate family interpolating from CZ to iSWAP via the B gate. This work allows the implementation of any two-qubit gate natively in neutral-atom platforms, enabling flexible switching between instruction sets to reduce circuit depth and compilation overhead in quantum algorithm implementation.

item.title: The energetic cost of loading classical data in quantum computers
item.description:
Skim theory — Querying a 12-qubit address bucket-brigade QRAM achieves fidelity 0.969 while consuming 3.51×10−4J dynamic energy, averaging 4.38W dynamic power with 64.4W peak.

Grade 0.474 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Noise-Adaptive Compiler Mappings for Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum Computers” · Joao F. Doriguello, Alessandro Luongo, Harshit Verma

Asks

What is the physical dynamic energetic cost of loading classical data via QRAM architectures on superconducting quantum hardware?

But

Theoretical and numerical optimization model assuming transmon superconducting gates; accounts for dynamic drive power, thermal photons, and attenuation profiles, excluding static cryostat cooling overhead.

Tools

metric-noise-resource framework · bucket-brigade QRAM architecture · linear-depth multiplexer QRAM · superconducting gate decomposition schedule · multi-stage dilution refrigerator thermal model

Abstract

Quantum algorithms for machine learning, chemistry, and cryptanalysis often assume coherent access to classical data at negligible physical cost. We instead treat data loading as a hardware process and quantify the dynamic energetic cost of a quantum random access memory (QRAM) query on a superconducting processor. Using the metric-noise-resource framework, we relate query fidelity and power to gate duration, relative two-qubit drive strength, and the distribution of attenuation across a multi-stage refrigerator, while accounting for thermal photons and gate errors. We analyze the linear-depth multiplexer and the noise-resilient bucket-brigade architectures, adapting the latter to a native superconducting gate set and refining its fidelity analysis using the fully decomposed gate schedule. For a representative bucket-brigade QRAM query with a 12-qubit address register we obtain a query fidelity of 0.969. The query consumes 3.51×10⁻⁴ J of dynamic energy, corresponding to an average dynamic power of 4.38 W and a peak of 64.4 W. Our optimization shows that, at fixed target fidelity, the operating point and attenuation profile can change the average power by a factor of two or more.
